questions.q: A user logs in to a site over plain http while on an open Wifi network, and an attacker on the same network learns the password. Which risk is this?
choices: Eavesdropping
Online guessing attack
Client-side malware
Server compromise
questions.explain: The password was sent in cleartext over an unencrypted connection, so anyone who could listen on the network could read it.

questions.q: An attacker steals a site's database of cleartext passwords. Why does this also put users' accounts on other websites at risk?
choices: Users often reuse the same password across multiple sites
All websites share a single password database
Cleartext passwords reveal the other sites' TLS keys
Stolen passwords let the attacker forge other sites' CAPTCHAs
questions.explain: Many users reuse one password across sites because it is easier to remember, so a breach on one site helps the attacker log in elsewhere.

questions.q: What is the standard, straightforward defense against eavesdroppers learning passwords in transit?
choices: Connect over SSL/TLS (https) so the username and password travel over an encrypted channel
Hash the password with SHA256 on the server before storing it
Add a random salt to each user's password
Rate-limit login attempts
questions.explain: https encrypts the connection, so an eavesdropper can't read the password. Hashing, salting and rate-limiting address other threats.

questions.q: In a challenge-response login, the server sends a random challenge r and the browser sends back H(w, r), where w is the password. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The password itself never crosses the network, but the scheme offers little or no advantage over SSL, so SSL remains the standard defense
It sends the password encrypted under r, so only the server can decrypt it
It is strictly stronger than SSL and has replaced SSL on most login pages
It cannot be implemented in a web browser
questions.explain: Only H(w, r) is sent, which stops eavesdroppers. It could be done today with JavaScript, but it has little or no advantage over SSL and some drawbacks, so SSL is used instead.

questions.q: A randomized on-screen virtual keyboard (keys shuffled, user clicks the characters) is an effective defense against client-side malware.
questions.explain: It only beats a keylogger that records keystrokes. Malware can easily record where each mouse click lands and take a screenshot on every click.

questions.q: If your computer has malware on it and you type in your password, the attacker learns it. What is the main defense in this threat model?
choices: Two-factor authentication, combining the password with another factor such as an SMS sent to your phone
Choosing a longer, more random password
Logging in only over https
Using a randomized on-screen keyboard
questions.explain: Passwords are basically insecure against client-side malware. A second factor means the stolen password alone is not enough to log in.

questions.q: According to measurement studies, about what percentage of users' passwords can be found with a dictionary of just the 10 most common passwords?
questions.explain: About 1% of users choose a password from the top 10 most common passwords.

questions.q: About what percentage of users' passwords can be guessed with a dictionary of the 2^20 (about one million) most common passwords?
questions.explain: About half of all users have a password that is in the 2^20 most common passwords.

questions.q: An attacker wants to take over any existing Gmail account to send spam, and doesn't care whose account it is. What kind of attack is this?
choices: Untargeted attack
Targeted attack
Amortized guessing attack
Eavesdropping attack
questions.explain: In an untargeted attack the attacker just needs some user's password. In a targeted attack they want one particular user's password.

questions.q: In an untargeted online attack, the attacker tries the 10 most common passwords against each account on a long list. About how many login attempts in total should they expect to make before guessing one password correctly?
questions.explain: 10 guesses succeed about 1% of the time, so they need about 100 accounts x 10 guesses = about 1000 attempts. This can be automated, so resistance to untargeted attacks is very low.

questions.q: In a targeted online attack where each login attempt takes 1 second, about how long does it take to make 2^20 guesses?
choices: About 11 hours
About 11-12 days
About 1 year
About 24 years
questions.explain: 2^20 seconds is about one million seconds, roughly 11-12 days. An attack like this is also very noticeable and easy for the server to detect.

questions.q: A targeted online attacker who makes 2^20 guesses at one user's password is essentially guaranteed to succeed.
questions.explain: 2^20 guesses cover only about half of users. If the attacker is unlucky it can take far more guesses, so a targeted attack is possible but not guaranteed.

questions.q: A site limits each account to 5 incorrect guesses per hour. At least how many years would a targeted attacker need to make 2^20 guesses?
questions.explain: 2^20 / 5 = about 210,000 hours, which is about 24 years. That makes at least half of users essentially immune to targeted attacks.

questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of locking an account after too many incorrect login attempts?
choices: It enables denial of service: Mallory can deliberately enter wrong passwords until Bob's account is locked
It lets attackers test guesses offline
It forces the server to store passwords in the clear
It makes eavesdropping easier
questions.explain: Rate-limiting lets anyone lock someone else's account. In many settings that risk is acceptable.

questions.q: Why is rate-limiting not an effective defense against untargeted attacks?
choices: The attacker spreads a few guesses (even one) across many accounts, so no account hits the limit, yet some account still falls
Untargeted attackers always switch to offline guessing
Rate limits only apply to accounts with weak passwords
Rate limits can be bypassed by connecting over https
questions.explain: For example, 5 guesses against each of 200 accounts, or 1 guess against each of 1000 accounts, is expected to break into at least one, and a rate limit won't stop 5 guesses or even 1.

questions.q: After a failed login on an account, a site requires a CAPTCHA for the next attempt on that account, so n guesses at one account need n-1 CAPTCHAs. An attacker makes 10 guesses at each of 100 accounts. How many CAPTCHAs must they solve?
questions.explain: 9 CAPTCHAs per account x 100 accounts = 900. At black-market rates that costs maybe a dollar or two. One guess at each of 1000 accounts would need no CAPTCHAs at all.

questions.q: Why do CAPTCHAs add less protection against automated password guessing than one might hope?
choices: Black-market services pay low-wage human workers to solve them for about $1-2 per thousand, with APIs that automate the process
Most humans cannot solve CAPTCHAs
CAPTCHAs are only shown after the account is already locked
CAPTCHAs only work when the connection uses http rather than https
questions.explain: At about 0.1-0.2 cents per CAPTCHA, they make a targeted attack cost more but not impossible, and they do not stop untargeted attacks.

questions.q: What gentle 'nudge' has been found to encourage people to choose longer, stronger passwords, without imposing hard requirements?
choices: Showing a password strength meter during account creation
Locking the account after 5 failed guesses
Requiring a CAPTCHA at signup
Forcing a password change every 30 days
questions.explain: Studies found that just showing a password meter during account creation helps people choose longer and stronger passwords.

questions.q: Stringent password-composition rules (e.g., at least 10 characters with a number and a symbol) reliably improve security because users comply with them.
questions.explain: Such rules are hard to use and frustrate users, who may try to get around them, so they may not help security at all.

questions.q: With simple password hashing, the server stores H(w) for Alice's password w. When Alice logs in with password w', how does the server check it?
choices: It computes H(w') and checks whether it matches the stored H(w)
It inverts the stored H(w) to recover w and compares it with w'
It decrypts the stored hash with the server's secret key
It sends H(w) to the browser and lets the browser compare
questions.explain: Hash functions are one-way, so the server never recovers w. It hashes the submitted password and compares the two hashes.

questions.q: Mallory steals a database of password hashes. What makes her attack an 'offline' guessing attack?
choices: She tests each guess g by computing H(g) on her own computer and comparing it to the stolen hash, with no further interaction with the website
She only guesses while the website is down
She must still submit each guess to the login page, but from a disconnected machine
She reads the cleartext passwords directly from the database
questions.explain: Each guess is checked locally, so login-page defenses like rate-limiting and CAPTCHAs don't apply.

questions.q: A site with 100 million users stores unsalted SHA256 password hashes. An attacker can compute about 1 billion SHA256 hashes per second and tries 2^20 guesses against each user one by one. About how long does this take?
choices: About 100 seconds
About a day
About a year
About 3000 machine-years
questions.explain: 100 million x 2^20 = about 100 trillion guesses. At 10^9 per second that is about 10^5 seconds, roughly a day, and it reveals about half the users' passwords.

questions.q: With unsalted hashes, why can an attacker hash each candidate password only once and check the result against every user?
choices: H(w) doesn't depend on the user, so any two users with the same password have the same hash
SHA256 is easy to invert for short inputs
The database also stores each user's password in the clear
Each user's hash is encrypted under the same server key
questions.explain: This is the amortized guessing attack. Build a sorted list of (H(g), g) for the 2^20 most common passwords, then look up each user's hash with binary search.

questions.q: In the amortized guessing attack, the attacker sorts a list of 2^20 (H(g), g) pairs by hash value. About how many random accesses does a binary search need to check one user's hash against this list?
questions.explain: Binary search over 2^20 entries takes about lg(2^20) = 20 steps. The whole attack takes about 2^20 hashes (about a millisecond), a sort, and one fast lookup per user.

questions.q: What is the name for the random, non-secret, per-user value that is hashed together with the password and stored next to the hash?
questions.explain: The server stores s and H(w, s). The salt's only purpose is to be different for each user.

questions.q: For salting to be effective, each user's salt must be kept secret from anyone who steals the database.
questions.explain: The salt is stored in cleartext and the attacker will see it. What matters is that each user's salt is different, so work done for one user can't be reused for another.

questions.q: Which attack does adding a random per-user salt defeat?
choices: The amortized guessing attack: the attacker can no longer hash each candidate once and reuse the result for every user
All offline guessing, including guesses against a single user's hash
Eavesdropping on the login connection
Online guessing through the login page
questions.explain: With salts s_A and s_B, the attacker must compute H(g_i, s_A) for Alice and a completely new set H(g_i, s_B) for Bob. Guessing a single user's password offline still works.

questions.q: Storing a random salt with a single SHA256 hash is enough to make offline guessing impractical after a database breach.
questions.explain: SHA256 is fast, so trying 2^20 guesses against each of 100 million salted hashes still takes about a day. After LinkedIn's breach of SHA256 hashes, one researcher recovered 90% of passwords in 6 days. You also need a slow hash.

questions.q: To slow down a fast hash H, define F(x) = H(H(...H(x)...)), applying H n times. Which statement is true?
choices: F is still a good cryptographic hash and is about n times slower than H, so n is a tunable slowness parameter
F is weaker than H because iterating a hash destroys its one-way property
F is only slower for the server, not for an attacker
F is only slow if it is computed with a secret key
questions.explain: Iterated hashing lets you choose how slow the hash is. The attacker must evaluate F for every guess, just like the server.

questions.q: What is the tradeoff when choosing the iteration count n for a slow password hash?
choices: A larger n slows offline guessing more, but the server must also evaluate F on every login attempt, so pick the largest n whose overhead is still unnoticeable
A larger n makes hash collisions between users more likely
n must equal the number of users so that salts stay unique
A smaller n is more secure because it gives attackers less time to observe the server
questions.explain: Security calls for a large n, and server performance calls for a small one. Choose the most security you can get while keeping the cost unnoticeable.

questions.q: A busy site expects at most 10 logins per second and tunes its slow hash F so that one evaluation takes 1 millisecond. About what percentage of the server's CPU goes to password hashing?
questions.explain: 10 logins x 1 ms = 10 ms of hashing per second, which is 1% of CPU. Meanwhile, trying 2^20 guesses against all 100 million users would take the attacker about 3000 machine-years instead of a day.

questions.q: Which of these are existing slow-hashing schemes meant for storing passwords?
choices: Scrypt
Bcrypt
PBKDF2
SHA256
AES
questions.explain: Scrypt, Bcrypt and PBKDF2 all use some form of iterated hashing. SHA256 is a fast hash, which is the problem, and AES is a block cipher, not a hash.

questions.q: For a user with password w, what is the recommended thing for a server to store?
choices: s, H(H(...H(w, s)...)): a random per-user salt plus a slow, iterated hash of the password and salt
s, H(w, s) computed with a single SHA256
H(w), the SHA256 hash of the password
w, protected by database access controls
questions.explain: Never store passwords in the clear. Use a random salt to defeat amortized attacks and a slow hash to make each offline guess expensive.

questions.q: A file-encryption tool asks for a password w and encrypts the file under the key k = H(w), where H is SHA256. What is the main weakness?
choices: An attacker can hash the 2^20 most common passwords, try decrypting with each key, and check whether the result looks like plaintext. This is very fast and works about half the time
Hashing makes the key different each time the user types the password, so the file can't be decrypted later
SHA256 can easily be inverted to recover w from the ciphertext
The key has to be sent to a server, which exposes it to eavesdroppers
questions.explain: Password-derived keys inherit how guessable the password is. Since SHA256 is fast, the whole dictionary attack takes about a millisecond.

questions.q: The same file-encryption tool switches to a slow hash tuned to take 1 ms per evaluation. Roughly how many minutes does an attacker need to try all 2^20 most common passwords?
questions.explain: The attacker can make 1000 guesses per second, and 2^20 ms is about 1049 s, roughly 15-17 minutes, for about a 50% chance of breaking the encryption. A slow hash helps, but not enough.

questions.q: Instead of deriving cryptographic keys from passwords or passphrases, what is the better practice?
choices: Use a truly random key (e.g., a random 128-bit AES key) and find a secure way for the user to store it
Derive the key by hashing the password twice with SHA256
Require the passphrase to be at least 10 characters with a number and a symbol
Use the password itself directly as the AES key
questions.explain: Keys derived from passwords tend to be weak, so avoid them when possible. A truly random key can't be found with a dictionary of likely passwords.

questions.q: Which of these are alternatives to passwords for authenticating to a server?
choices: Two-factor authentication
One-time PINs (e.g., a single-use SMS code or an RSA SecurID device)
Public-key cryptography (e.g., SSH)
Secure persistent cookies
Randomized on-screen virtual keyboards
Stricter password-composition rules
questions.explain: Virtual keyboards and composition rules still depend entirely on a password, and both have weaknesses of their own.
